articles.headline: Amazon's Cloud Booms, Its Cash Goes Negative, and Wall Street Chooses to Be Upset
articles.dek: Shares fell more than 6% after hours as AWS grew 39% but capital spending hit $77.3 billion in one quarter and free cash flow turned deeply negative.
articles.catch_up: Amazon reported third-quarter results on Thursday showing faster cloud growth, weaker retail and advertising, and a spending bill for AI data centers that keeps climbing. Microsoft and Alphabet reported earlier in the week, with their own cloud businesses also accelerating.
articles.why_it_matters: Amazon is one of the largest companies in major stock indexes, so a market that doubts AI spending will pay off affects anyone with a retirement fund. The quarter is a reminder that the AI boom is currently funded by enormous cash outflows, with the returns promised for later.
body: Amazon shares fell more than 6% in extended trading Thursday after the company reported third-quarter earnings of $1.89 per share against the $1.96 analysts expected, according to CNBC. Revenue was $201.94 billion, just under the $202.31 billion forecast. The company's cloud unit beat expectations, which is the sort of news that normally ends well, and did not.

The cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, brought in $45.98 billion, up 39% from a year earlier, against a $45.29 billion forecast. CNBC said that is the fastest growth since the fourth quarter of 2021, and AWS operating income rose 55% to $17.77 billion. AWS now makes up almost 23% of Amazon's revenue, a record. Translation: the part of Amazon that rents computers to other companies is working well enough that it is slowly becoming the company.

The trouble is the price of the computers. Capital expenditures, or capex (Translation: money spent on buildings, servers and other things you cannot return), reached $77.3 billion in the quarter, up from $35.1 billion a year earlier and well above the $58.7 billion analysts expected, according to FactSet. Amazon held its 2026 capex forecast at $220 billion. Microsoft trimmed its own forecast to $170 billion from $175 billion this week, and Alphabet held at $195 billion to $205 billion.

The result is negative free cash flow (Translation: more cash going out than coming in, after paying for the equipment). Amazon recorded an outflow of $42.4 billion over the trailing twelve months, a 386% swing from a year ago, and the second straight quarter in the red. The company said the shortfall was mainly due to AI-related purchases of property and equipment. The prior quarter's figure was a negative $7.6 billion, so the trend line has a certain confidence to it.

Elsewhere in the building, things were softer. Online sales rose 2% to $68.47 billion, missing the $69.68 billion estimate and slowing from nearly 10% growth a year earlier. Advertising rose 11% to $19.64 billion, short of the $20.82 billion consensus. Amazon moved its Prime Day sale into the second quarter in several countries to avoid clashing with the FIFA World Cup, which CNBC said affected both units. Even a shopping holiday has to check the sports calendar.

Fourth-quarter guidance of $240 billion to $247 billion has a midpoint below the $244.5 billion Wall Street wanted, according to LSEG. That is a modest miss for the holiday quarter, but investors in a spending race tend to read every small gap as a statement about the large one.

CEO Andy Jassy offered reassurance on the call. He said Amazon has a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns, expects AWS growth of over 40% in 2027 and 2028, and sees AWS becoming a $1 trillion revenue business in five to 10 years. He also said Amazon expects to spend meaningfully more in 2027, which is the kind of sentence that makes the first half of the previous one do a lot of work. Trainium, Amazon's in-house AI chip, will be offered outside AWS late in 2027, a strategy Google has used with its own chips, according to CNBC.

The market's message is a familiar one: growth is welcome, but it must arrive before the invoice. For now, Amazon is a company with a faster-growing cloud, a bigger bill and a thinner cushion. The next test is whether 2027's larger spending produces the 40% growth that is currently on the slide deck.
articles.wire_headline: Amazon’s stock drops — even in the face of a bold new cloud forecast

articles.headline: Intel Beats Estimates, Then Falls 21% After Telling Investors What Comes Next
articles.dek: The chipmaker posted a strong third quarter, but a weak forecast tied to soaring memory prices and a fatal factory explosion sent shares down more than 20% after hours.
articles.catch_up: Intel has been one of the year's big stock winners, up about 150% before Thursday's report, as investors bet on AI demand for its server chips and its revival as a U.S. manufacturer. The company reported third-quarter results on Thursday alongside guidance for the current quarter.
articles.why_it_matters: Memory shortages created by AI data centers are now raising costs for laptops and slowing PC sales, which means the AI buildout is showing up in ordinary consumer electronics. Investors holding Intel after a 150% run learned how quickly a forecast can undo a good quarter.
body: Intel shares fell more than 20% in extended trading on Thursday after the company gave a fourth-quarter forecast well below what analysts expected, CNBC reported. This came after a quarter that beat expectations. The market, as usual, paid for the future rather than the past, and the future was marked down.

The quarter itself was solid. Revenue rose 21% to $16.51 billion, in line with the $16.5 billion analysts expected, and adjusted earnings were 52 cents per share against 40 cents expected, according to LSEG figures cited by CNBC. Data center and AI revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion. Translation: the part of Intel that sells to AI builders is doing wonderfully, and the part that sells to people who own laptops is not.

The guidance is where it went wrong. Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and adjusted earnings of 25 cents per share. Analysts had pencilled in $17.1 billion and 43 cents. Translation: guidance is the company's own prediction of its next three months, and investors treat it as the only part of the earnings report that matters.

The cause is memory. Revenue in Intel's client computing group, which covers PCs, fell 5% to $8.1 billion and missed estimates. Counterpoint Research said global PC shipments fell 4% in the second quarter on soaring memory and component costs. CNBC's Investing Club commentary explained the mechanism: data center builders can raise money by issuing debt or selling equity and will pay whatever memory costs, while consumers and corporate IT departments cannot. Both groups draw on the same limited factory capacity, and the people with the bond market behind them are winning.

CEO Lip-Bu Tan said customers began signaling a PC slowdown in recent weeks, based on memory prices and availability. He also described one of the most significant supply shortages in history. Finance chief David Zinsner said the PC slowdown should continue at least through the first half of next year. Nobody on the call suggested the shortage was caused by anything other than the industry's own enthusiasm.

There was also a human cost that the earnings call had to account for. An explosion at an Intel fab in Israel earlier this month killed two workers and seriously injured a third. Tan called it an unfortunate and tragic accident. It has caused an extended shutdown at the plant, affecting shipments of 10-nanometer chips. Zinsner put the cost at about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, while the Investing Club piece cited roughly $300 million in the fourth quarter and a similar amount in the first.

The long-term case remains intact, at least in management's telling. Intel estimates agentic AI, where software agents run tasks in the cloud and lean on CPUs, could expand the server CPU market from $40 billion to as much as $200 billion in five years. Its 18A chip is in high-volume production in Arizona, but it still has no major outside customers for it. Tan said a couple of customers could be announced over the next two quarters. The company's foundry external revenue was $411 million, which CNBC's Investing Club noted was boosted by a non-recurring program.

The stock had already fallen about 23% in October on worries about the size of the AI buildout, so Thursday's drop landed on a lot of nervous holders. Nvidia reports in mid-November and AMD reports next week, which will test whether Intel's problem is its own or the whole sector's. For now, the AI boom has successfully made chips more valuable and laptops more expensive, and Intel sells both.
articles.wire_headline: Intel stock plunges 21% as chipmaker blames PC slowdown for weak guidance

articles.headline: Economy Grows 3.4% as Inflation Also Grows, Fed Promises to Keep Looking at Both
articles.dek: Third-quarter GDP beat forecasts and jobless claims sat near 1960s lows, but September prices rose 0.5% and the Fed has chosen to study the matter further.
articles.catch_up: The Commerce Department reported Thursday that U.S. GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, while the Fed's preferred inflation gauge hit 3.6% for the year. The Fed held rates at 3.75%-4% the day before.
articles.why_it_matters: Strong growth with inflation well above the Fed's 2% target makes rate cuts harder to justify, and borrowing costs may stay high for longer. Energy-driven price increases hit household budgets directly, whatever the headline growth number says.
body: The U.S. economy grew at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, beating the 3.1% forecast and the 2.2% of the second quarter, the Commerce Department reported Thursday, according to CNBC. The same morning brought news that inflation had accelerated in September. The economy, in other words, is doing better and costing more, which is a combination most households recognize from the grocery store.

The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's favored inflation gauge, rose 0.5% in September and 3.6% from a year earlier. Translation: prices are climbing at a rate the central bank describes as a target overshoot, a phrase that means 'we said 2%, and this is not that.' Core PCE, which strips out food and energy because the Fed assumes you can live without both, rose 0.3% for the month and 3.1% for the year. Both readings matched forecasts.

The culprit was energy. Gasoline and other energy goods rose 9.2% in the month, and energy goods and services overall rose 5.4%. Economists, CNBC reported, worry the increase could spread to other parts of the economy. Services excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, which suggests the worry is not purely theoretical. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, was most recently at $123.10, which suggests relief is not imminent.

The growth itself leaned heavily on the artificial intelligence build-out. Gross private domestic investment jumped 19.4%, with equipment spending up 20.9% and intellectual property products up 8.4%. Translation: companies are buying a great deal of hardware and software to prepare for a future in which they will need less of other things. Consumer spending rose 3.8%, the same pace as the prior quarter, and real sales to private domestic purchasers, which the Fed treats as a gauge of underlying demand, rose 4.9%.

The labor market offered no argument. Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the 200,000 forecast and near levels last seen in the late 1960s. Unemployment stood at 4.2% as of the latest official reading. Few people are being laid off, which means few people are available to be talked into accepting lower inflation.

There was some mild good news. On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% overall and 2.5% for core, down from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. Chris Rupkey of Fwdbonds said growth was 'powering ahead' despite geopolitical risks and higher energy costs. The quarter looked better than September, which is a bit like praising a restaurant's average meal after a bad dessert.

The Fed, for its part, held its benchmark rate at 3.75%-4% on Wednesday. Chairman Kevin Warsh said the period ahead is 'information rich' and that he and colleagues are keen to take notice of it. Thursday's data was a great deal of information, and most of it points toward the Fed having more work to do. Markets reacted accordingly: stock futures fell and Treasury yields declined, though the 10-year yield at 5.05% is hardly a bargain.

What to watch next is whether energy costs keep leaking into everything else. If they do, the Fed's careful evaluation of incoming data will end with a conclusion it could probably have drafted this week.
articles.wire_headline: Third-quarter U.S. GDP increases a better-than-expected 3.4% as September inflation accelerates
